An ingot is a solid block of metal that has been melted down and poured into a mold to harden into a simple, convenient shape — usually a rectangle or a bar — so it can be stored, transported, or processed further.

Think of it this way: imagine you collected a huge pile of scrap metal — old car parts, broken tools, metal scraps of all shapes and sizes. That pile is messy, uneven, and nearly impossible to measure, store neatly, or work with. Now imagine you melt all of it down into a liquid and pour it into a rectangular brick mold, like an ice cube tray, and let it cool. What you get when it hardens is an ingot — a clean, solid, uniform block of metal that is easy to handle.

An ingot is most commonly shaped like a rectangular brick or a thick bar. It is deliberately kept in this plain, simple shape because the goal is not to make something decorative or functional yet — the goal is just to make the metal manageable. Think of the classic gold bars you see in movies stacked inside a bank vault. Those are gold ingots. They are smooth, dense, heavy, and shaped like thick bricks.

The size and weight of an ingot can vary enormously depending on its purpose. A gold ingot held in bank vaults (called a "good delivery" bar) weighs about 400 troy ounces — roughly 12.4 kilograms, or 27 pounds. But smaller ingots can weigh just a few grams. On the industrial end, steel ingots used in factories can weigh several tonnes.

The process is straightforward:

  1. Metal is heated in a furnace until it melts into a liquid.
  2. The liquid metal is poured into a mold — a container shaped like a brick, bar, or block.
  3. It is left to cool and solidify, hardening into that shape.
  4. The solid block is removed from the mold. That block is the ingot.

This is sometimes called casting. The mold determines the shape, and the shape is always kept simple on purpose.
What Metals Are Made Into Ingots?

Almost any metal can be formed into an ingot. The most commonly known ones are:

  • Gold — the classic image of wealth stored as ingots in vaults
  • Silver — similarly stored and traded as ingots
  • Steel — massively produced in industry for making cars, buildings, and machines
  • Aluminum — widely used ingots that get turned into countless products
  • Copper — used in electrical and industrial applications
  • Platinum and other precious metals
Why Do Ingots Exist? What's the Point?

Ingots exist because they solve a practical problem: how do you store, move, and measure metal efficiently?

Raw ore dug from the ground is full of impurities and comes in irregular lumps. Scrap metal is all different shapes and sizes. Neither is easy to work with. An ingot solves this by giving metal a clean, standardized form. Here's why that matters:

  • Storage: Rectangular blocks stack neatly and take up predictable space.
  • Transport: A uniform shape is far easier to move and load than irregular chunks.
  • Measurement: Because an ingot is one solid piece, its weight and purity can be measured and certified. This is critical in trade — a gold ingot can be stamped with its weight and purity so buyers know exactly what they are getting.
  • Further manufacturing: Factories need metal in a clean, ready-to-use form. An ingot is that form. It can be melted again and reshaped into specific products.
The Ingot's Role in the Bigger Picture

An ingot is essentially a middle step in the life of metal. It sits between raw ore (the beginning) and a finished product (the end).

Raw ore → Ingot → Finished product

For example, aluminum ore is mined, refined, and cast into aluminum ingots. Those ingots are then sent to factories where they are melted again, rolled into sheets, and eventually turned into airplane parts, drink cans, window frames, or kitchen foil.

The ingot itself is not a final product. Nobody uses an ingot directly in their daily life. It is an intermediate, standardized form of metal waiting to be turned into something else.

Ingots — especially gold and silver ones — have historically been used as a form of stored wealth and traded commodity. Because an ingot has a measurable, certifiable weight and purity, it can be bought and sold like a financial asset. Central banks around the world hold gold ingots in their reserves. Investors buy silver ingots as a store of value. In this context, an ingot is almost like a very heavy, very dense coin — a universally understood unit of valuable metal.

An ingot is a block of metal made by melting metal down and letting it harden in a mold into a simple shape, created purely for the practical purpose of making metal easy to store, transport, trade, and process further.
